summary: Supply the car cost, the average distance traveled and the distance traveled and the Plug-in hybrid economy calculator solves for trips per month (Trips shorter than battery range). Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Plug-in hybrid economy calculator work?
sections.html:
The Plug-in hybrid economy calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports trips per month (Trips shorter than battery range) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the car model); then you type in the car cost, the average distance traveled (Trips shorter than battery range), the distance traveled (Trips shorter than battery range) and the average distance traveled (Trips longer than battery range).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Plug-in hybrid economy calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Trips per month=distance traveled ÷ average distance traveled
Total distance traveled=distance traveled + distance traveled
Distance on battery=distance traveled + trips per month × range on battery
Total distance traveled=distance on battery + distance on gas
Your MPG=3370 × MPG (gas only) × total distance traveled ÷ (consumption rate × MPG (gas only) × distance on battery + 3370 × distance on gas)
Gas price=expenses (gas) × MPG of a regular car ÷ total distance traveled

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Length, opening in miles
  • Fuel economy, opening in liters per 100 kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Plug-in hybrid economy calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the car cost, the average distance traveled and the distance traveled — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Plug-in hybrid economy calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns trips per month (Trips shorter than battery range), derived from the car cost, the average distance traveled and the distance traveled. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Plug-in hybrid economy calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the car cost, the average distance traveled and the distance traveled, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter range on battery in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Range on battery opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Range on battery = 0 km. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Plug-in hybrid economy calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
